segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, passionate, sometimes argumentative journey through one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be reading Dickens's masterpiece — chapter by chapter, image by image, character by magnificent character.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the fog.

Bleak House opens with one of the most arresting pages in Victorian fiction — a London so wrapped in fog and mud that you can barely see your hand in front of your face, let alone the truth of anything.
And that fog, we'll be arguing today, is doing enormous work — aesthetic, moral, political, spiritual.
To explore it, I have three extraordinary companions.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens scholars of his generation — a man who believes the novel's greatness lives in its moral imagination, in character rather than polemic.
Edmund, wonderful to have you.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he has spoken these sentences aloud thousands of times and knows exactly where every laugh and every silence lives in the prose.
Oliver, delighted you're here.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a literary critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since — she brings the reader's eye, the lover's attention, and occasionally the reader's fury on behalf of characters who deserve better.
Caroline, welcome.
Let's begin exactly where Dickens begins — in the fog.
The thing about reading that opening aloud — and I've read it, I should think, a hundred and fifty times in various forms — is that it doesn't feel like a novel beginning.
It feels like the curtain going up on an enormous stage that's full of smoke.
Dickens doesn't give you a character, a date, a household.
He gives you weather — and the weather is somehow moral.
The passage starts — and you must hear it to believe it — with London in November.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That word — defiled — sitting right next to meadows and green aits.
That's not accidental.
Dickens is already telling you that the city corrupts, that contact with it — even for a river — leaves a mark.
Oliver is quite right about the theatrical quality, and I wouldn't quarrel with the observation about corruption — so far as it goes.
But I think we should be careful not to flatten this extraordinary passage into a simple diagram — city bad, country good.
The fog is everywhere, after all.
It reaches — and Dickens is quite specific — into the Essex marshes, the Kentish heights.
It is not a metropolitan affliction only.
What Dickens is constructing, I would argue, is an image of universal obscuration — of moral blindness that belongs to no one class, no one institution.
He then brings that fog indoors — and this is the masterstroke — into the High Court of Chancery itself.
"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery."
Groping and floundering — these are not the words of a polemicist.
These are the words of a moralist — someone interested in what darkness does to the soul, not merely to the statute book.
I want to come back to something Oliver said — that it feels like a curtain going up.
Because I think what's so remarkable — and what I notice every time I reread this opening — is how Dickens keeps withholding.
We don't see anyone for pages.
We see dogs, loosened from their owners.
We see a hypothetical megalosaurus waddling up Holborn Hill — which is one of the most extraordinary opening images in all of fiction, if you stop to think about it.
A prehistoric monster on a London street.
Dickens says it wouldn't feel particularly surprising — and he means that.
The fog has made the present prehistoric — it has undone time.
And then Edmund's point about Chancery — yes, absolutely — but what moves me is the line just before that.
"At the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery."
At the very heart of it.
The fog doesn't drift into Chancery accidentally.
Chancery is where the fog originates.
Caroline, that's exactly right — and it's there in the rhythm, too.
The sentence — "Fog everywhere" — is two words.
That's it.
After that, you get these rolling, accumulating clauses — up the river, down the river, on the Essex marshes, on the Kentish heights — and they go on and on until you feel the fog in your lungs.
Dickens wrote to be read aloud.
This is performance — it's designed to exhaust you slightly, to make you feel that there is no escape, no gap in the fog through which you might slip.
And then of course you get — and I confess this never ceases to delight me — the Lord Chancellor himself, with his foggy glory and his foggy solicitors and his foggy suitors.
"Foggy glory around his lordship's head."
It's magnificent and it's absurd and it's entirely serious — all at once.
That's the genius of it.
I'm glad Oliver mentions the absurdity, because I think this is where the purely political reading begins to strain.
If the fog were simply a denunciation of the legal system — if it were journalism — it would not be funny.
But the Lord Chancellor sitting in his foggy glory is comic — and Dickens knows it.
Comedy, Dr. Johnson reminds us, is a mirror held up to the follies of mankind.
Dickens holds up the mirror very high — high enough to catch not just Chancery but the whole of human self-delusion.
What the fog hides, ultimately, is not a conspiracy but a condition — the condition of not seeing clearly.
And what the novel then asks — brilliantly — is which of these characters will find their way through it, and which will be consumed.
That question of who finds their way through it — I think it haunts the whole novel.
And it's worth saying: the fog isn't just atmospheric backdrop.
It returns — physically — throughout the novel.
Every time we enter Chancery, every time we move through Lincoln's Inn, we feel it close around us again.
And there's the counterpoint, which Dickens establishes almost immediately — Esther.
The moment Esther begins to narrate in her own voice — that clear, self-deprecating, utterly honest voice — the fog lifts, just slightly.
She says, "I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages" — and it's so quietly human that it cuts right through all that smoke.
Dickens has given us two narrators — the omniscient, fog-drenched, present-tense one; and Esther, who writes from memory, from survival.
That is an extraordinary structural decision.
That structural double vision — the fog-narrator and Esther — is something we'll be returning to throughout this series.
And Edmund's question — which characters find their way through the fog, and which are consumed — that is, in a very real sense, the shape of the whole novel.

In our next segment, we'll look at what Chancery actually is — and what it does to the people caught inside it: the Jarndyce inheritance, Richard Carstone, and the slow, terrible machinery of the law.
Stay with us.
We turn now to one of Bleak House's most painful portraits — Richard Carstone.
He arrives in the novel as a young man of charm and real promise — handsome, warm-hearted, genuinely loveable.
And yet Dickens arranges his destruction with the patience and inevitability of a Greek tragedy.
Edmund, I want to start with you — because I suspect you see Richard rather differently from the way the novel's social critics tend to frame him.
Quite differently, yes — and I think the difference matters enormously.
There is a persistent tendency in discussions of Richard Carstone to make him a victim — a victim of Chancery, of the system, of forces larger than himself.
And Dickens certainly provides the materials for that reading.
But I think it is — if I may put it plainly — a rather comfortable reading, and not the one Dickens is actually writing.
Richard has every advantage — the guardianship of Jarndyce, the love of Ada, the friendship of Esther.
He has, in Jarndyce, a man of exemplary wisdom and disinterested affection standing beside him at every turning.
What undoes Richard is not the Court of Chancery — it is the deficiency of will that Chancery merely reveals and accelerates.
Dickens gives us the key early, when Esther observes Richard's readiness to be pleased with any profession — surgeon, lawyer, soldier — with equal enthusiasm and equal brevity.
"He had been eight years at a public school and had learnt, I understood, to make Latin verses of several sorts, in the most admirable manner."
Dickens is being wicked there — that irony about the Latin verses cuts right to the heart of what Richard's education has and has not given him.
Edmund is absolutely right about the irony — and as someone who has read Richard aloud rather a lot, I can tell you that the prose itself betrays him.
Richard's sentences are always slightly too enthusiastic — they have the cadence of a man convincing himself.
Compare him to Jarndyce — whose sentences are measured, grounded, quietly absolute.
The moment I always find devastating — and I mean genuinely hard to get through in the recording booth — is when Richard tells Esther that his confidence in the suit is actually a form of duty.
He says — and this is in one of Esther's chapters, I believe around the middle of the book —
"I am disposed to think that there's something wrong somewhere, Ada, and that if we put it right, we shall find it was not quite so long as it appeared."
He is rationalising, of course — but the tragedy is that he half believes it.
And every time you read it, you want to shake him by the shoulders.
What strikes me every time I read the Richard sections is how Dickens refuses to make the decline melodramatic.
It's incremental — almost quiet.
Each time Esther visits him, he has become a little more hollow — a little more fixed on the suit, a little less present to the people who love him.
There's a passage that I come back to again and again — Esther describing Richard after he has thrown up his commission in the army.
She says something like — and I'm not quoting exactly — that he looked worn and haggard, but his eyes burned with that feverish light she had come to dread.
That image — the burning eyes in the wasted face — is Dickens showing us addiction.
The suit has become Richard's drug.
And what makes it unbearable is that Ada watches it happen, knowing that love alone cannot save him.
Caroline's point about the incremental decline is exactly right, and I would add that it has a very precise moral shape.
Richard does not simply drift — he makes choices.
The decision to abandon medicine, the decision to abandon the army, the decision to place himself in the hands of Vholes — these are acts of will, or rather failures of will enacted as acts of will.
And Vholes — one must speak of Vholes.
Dickens describes him as a man who seems to be always looking for a corpse — and that description, for once, I think, is not satirical hyperbole.
"Mr Vholes is a very respectable man. He has not a large business, but he is a very respectable man."
The repetition of 'respectable' — Dickens hammering that word until it bleeds — is a masterstroke of satirical prose.
But more to the point: Richard chooses Vholes. He prefers a lawyer who feeds his obsession to a guardian who would free him of it.
Vholes is one of the great monsters of English fiction — and Dickens hides the monstrousness so beautifully.
He has three daughters and an aged father in the Vale of Taunton — Dickens never lets you forget this.
It's a perfect comic grotesque — this funereal man with his black gloves and his slow professional speech, always invoking his dependants.
But then Dickens does this extraordinary thing where he pivots — and suddenly Vholes becomes genuinely frightening.
There's a moment — I believe it's when Esther visits Richard's chambers — where she sees Vholes with his hand on Richard's shoulder.
And the image Dickens creates is almost vampiric — Vholes feeding, Richard diminishing.
When I read that scene aloud, I always drop my voice — because suddenly the comedy is completely gone.
Oliver's word — vampiric — is exactly right.
And I think what makes the Richard plot so specifically modern — so uncomfortable — is that Vholes never lies to him.
He feeds Richard exactly what Richard wants: the validation that the suit is worth pursuing, that justice is almost within reach.
There's a heartbreaking exchange — I think in chapter fifty-something, quite late — where Richard says to Esther, almost with wonder:
"I have been in Court all day, and it's a very serious matter. But I am not cast down, I am not beaten yet."
He is spent.
He can barely stand.
And yet the fire is still there — that terrible, useless fire.
Dickens earns every tear in that scene.
I want to say something about the ending — Richard's death — because I think it is misread almost as often as his life is.
When Jarndyce and Jarndyce finally ends — consumed entirely by costs — Richard at first seems simply destroyed by the news.
But Dickens gives him a moment of clarity — a genuine, painful lucidity.
He says to Jarndyce — and this is the line I think the novel has been building towards —
"I will begin the world."
Three words.
And they are — one has to say — among the most devastating three words in all of Victorian fiction.
Because we know, as Richard perhaps does not quite know, that there is no world left to begin.
"I will begin the world" — I've read that line in three separate recordings and I still cannot get through it without stopping.
There's something about the simplicity of it — the childlike simplicity — that is almost unbearable.
Richard came into the novel as a boy, essentially — full of easy enthusiasms and no settled purpose.
And he dies as a boy — still believing, in his last moment, that the world might yet be begun.
Dickens writes Ada holding him — and the prose at that point is stripped bare.
No irony, no grotesquerie — just grief.
And Ada — I always want to make the case for Ada here.
She is often called passive, a cipher — but she chooses Richard when everyone she loves is begging her not to.
She marries him secretly, follows him into poverty, watches him dissolve — and never once reproaches him.
Esther finds her in that final scene — sitting beside Richard, this golden girl now pale and exhausted — and Dickens gives her only silence.
I think the silence is the point.
Ada's love has been absolute and it has not been enough — and Dickens does not flinch from that.
Richard Carstone — a character who is at once wholly of his time and entirely contemporary.
A man destroyed not by villainy but by the collision of a weak will with a system designed to exploit exactly that weakness.
Edmund, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to look at the fog itself — Dickens's great atmospheric invention, and what it might or might not mean.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Shadow: Plot and Deception

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the great engines of suspense in Bleak House — Lady Dedlock herself.
From the moment she appears, draped in that magnificent ennui of hers, the novel is haunted by what she knows and what she fears others will discover.
Dickens builds her story as a kind of slow detonation — we sense the fuse burning long before the explosion comes.
Caroline, you've described Lady Dedlock as the character who makes you hold your breath every time she appears. Where does that tension begin?
It begins almost before she speaks — in the way Dickens describes her stillness.
There's that extraordinary early portrait of her at Chesney Wold, bored, magnificent, apparently impenetrable.
And then — Tulkinghorn produces a legal document, and she sees the handwriting.
Dickens gives us the setup with such quiet precision. He writes something like —
"My Lady Dedlock has been bored to death. Concert, assembly, opera, theatre, drive, nothing is new to my Lady, under the worn-out heavens."
That refrain — 'my Lady' — it has this proprietorial distance, as if even the narrator keeps her at arm's length.
And then the handwriting shatters all of that composure, in a single paragraph.
That is when you understand that her boredom is armour, and it is suddenly failing her.
What strikes me is the moral architecture Dickens constructs around her.
Lady Dedlock is not a villain in any simple sense. She is a woman paying the compound interest on a single youthful transgression.
Burke wrote of the weight of the dead upon the living, and one feels something of that in Chesney Wold itself — that great house pressing down on her secret.
And Tulkinghorn — one of the genuinely sinister achievements of Victorian fiction — senses it immediately.
Dickens describes him as though introducing us to something geological — old, patient, implacable.
"He is of what is called the old school — a phrase generally meaning any school that seems never to have been young."
The comedy is perfectly targeted. Dickens understands that the most dangerous adversaries are those who have entirely outlived sentiment.
Against such a man, Lady Dedlock's pride is not merely a flaw — it is her only remaining weapon, and a fragile one.
Edmund is absolutely right about Tulkinghorn, but I want to dwell on the performance of it — because Dickens is staging this entire relationship theatrically.
Every scene between Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock is a kind of duel with the weapons hidden — nothing openly said, everything understood.
And she is extraordinary in those scenes — her replies are these perfectly turned acts of deflection.
When Tulkinghorn finally confronts her with what he knows, she asks him how he wishes to be paid for his silence.
And he tells her — he wants nothing. He simply wants her to remain exactly where she is, saying nothing, doing nothing.
That is his power — the power of the closed fist. And reading those pages aloud, you feel the walls of the room getting smaller.
Dickens describes that confrontation moment with something like —
"Give me no trouble, my Lady, and I will give you none. Remain as you are and all will be well."
It sounds almost civil, doesn't it. That is precisely why it's so completely monstrous.
And what's so affecting is that Lady Dedlock herself participates in the deception against her own self-interest — almost compulsively.
She could have confessed to Sir Leicester. Not early, perhaps, but even mid-novel — he might have borne it.
Instead she goes in disguise to find the grave of Hawdon — of Captain Nemo, the man she once loved.
That scene, in that dreadful burying ground, described through Jo's eyes — it undoes me every time.
Jo, who barely understands what he witnesses, leads this great lady through filth and darkness, and Dickens frames it as —
"She is dressed in plain clothes, but she is not like the other people. She does not speak to him except to say what she wants."
Even in extremity, even in grief, she cannot stop performing.
And that, to me, is the tragedy. The mask has been worn so long she can no longer find her face beneath it.
Caroline touches on something I consider central to the novel's moral vision — the question of whether concealment is itself a kind of corruption.
Lady Dedlock is not a wicked woman. But she has lived in falsehood so long that the truth, when it must emerge, destroys not only the secret but the person who held it.
And Dickens is careful — he does not condemn her. He mourns her.
Her letter to Esther — left behind before the final flight — is one of the most restrained and therefore most devastating things in the book.
She writes, in terms that carry the full weight of a life lived at distance from truth —
"I have no home left. I am too dishonoured to remain where I have been so long, or to see the people among whom I have moved."
The word 'moved' — to move among people, to circulate in society. That is all she has had. And now it is forfeit.
The social self collapses, and there is nothing beneath it to survive the fall.
What kills me — and I mean this as a reader, a performer, a human being — is the ending of her story.
She is found dead at the gate of the churchyard where Hawdon is buried, dressed in the clothes of Jenny the brickmaker's wife.
The greatest lady in England, died in a pauper's clothes, in a pauper's cemetery, reaching for the man she was not permitted to love.
Dickens gives us the discovery through Esther — and the language is spare, almost factual, which makes it completely unbearable.
She writes something very close to —
"I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face. And it was my mother, cold and dead."
I have read that sentence to audiences, on stage, in recording studios. It lands the same way every single time.
The monosyllables at the end — cold and dead. Dickens knew exactly what he was doing with those four words.
That sentence does something final — it closes the loop of a deception that has run through almost the entire novel.
And what's extraordinary is that even in death, Lady Dedlock remains a kind of mystery — to Esther, to the reader, to herself.
We'll carry her shadow with us as we move forward — there's much more in Bleak House that grows from the root of this concealment.

segments.title: The Crossing-Sweep's Witness: Dickens and Social Conscience

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, with Chancery, with the magnificent grotesques who orbit the Jarndyce case.
Now we turn to what many readers feel is the moral heart of the novel: Jo, the crossing-sweep.
A child who sweeps mud from the street crossing near Tom-all-Alone's — who knows nothing, who is taught nothing, and who dies of that nothing.
This segment is about Dickens the social conscience — what he was doing, whether it worked, and what it costs us as readers.
Edmund, you've always resisted the purely political reading of Bleak House — but Jo is a hard case to argue away from, isn't he?
I resist nothing so crude as arguing Jo away, I assure you.
Jo is one of the great achievements of Victorian fiction — precisely because Dickens refuses to sentimentalise him into a symbol.
He is a child with a particular voice, a particular bewilderment, a particular terrible dignity.
Consider the catechism scene — when Jo is asked before the inquest whether he understands the nature of an oath.
He says, and I think this is in chapter eleven: 'I don't know nothink.'
Three words — or rather, three words of negation — and Dickens has placed the entire weight of a society's failure on a child's tongue.
That is not sociology. That is moral imagination of the highest order.
Edmund is right about the dignity — and I'd add that Jo is also, technically, one of the funniest characters in the book.
Not funny in a cruel way — funny because Dickens gives him this absolutely precise, literal intelligence.
When Inspector Bucket tells him to move along — 'move on' is the great refrain — Jo says, essentially: I do move on, but I ain't got nowhere to move on to.
And that's both funny and devastating in the same breath — which is Dickens at the absolute peak of his craft.
When I read Jo aloud — and I've read him perhaps a hundred times — I always slow down at the 'move on' passages, because each one lands differently.
The repetition is doing structural work. It is the novel's heartbeat.
The 'move on' refrain — I want to dwell on that for a moment, because it's genuinely one of the most devastating verbal patterns in English fiction.
Dickens introduces it almost casually, as police procedure — just a constable doing his job.
But by the end of the novel it has become a kind of damnation.
There's a line — I believe it's in the chapter called 'Tom-all-Alone's' — where Dickens turns directly to the reader.
He writes something like: 'Jo is brought in. He is not one of Mrs. Jellyby's lambs, being wholly unconnected with Borrioboola-Gha; he is not softened by distance and unfamiliarity.'
That is Dickens drawing blood from his own satirical targets — the philanthropists who look anywhere but at the child in front of them.
It's savage, and it's precise, and it absolutely earns the emotion that follows.
Caroline touches on something I think is underappreciated — the structural sophistication of the novel's social critique.
Dickens does not simply indict the cruel. He indicts the well-meaning.
Mrs. Jellyby with her telescopic philanthropy, Mr. Quale with his missions to Africa — these people are not wicked.
They are morally distracted. And Dickens finds that almost more unforgivable.
Burke would have recognised the argument: the abstraction of human sympathy is always more comfortable than its concrete exercise.
Jo cannot be abstracted. He is standing right there, sweeping the crossing, asking for a penny.
And the extraordinary thing is that Dickens gives Jo almost no interiority at all.
We don't get inside Jo's head the way we get inside Esther's — he's almost entirely surface, speech, gesture.
And yet his death scene — when he's at George's shooting gallery, barely able to breathe — is among the most emotionally overwhelming pages Dickens ever wrote.
Woodcourt is trying to get Jo to repeat the Lord's Prayer, and Jo manages only fragments.
'The light is come upon the dark benighted way. Dead!'
And then Dickens breaks straight through the page — that famous direct address to Parliament, to the reader, to anyone who will listen.
I have read that passage aloud in theatres and I have never once got through it without the room going completely still.
That direct address is one of the great moments of radical authorial intrusion in the Victorian novel.
Dickens steps out of the fiction entirely and says — in effect — this is real. This is happening.
The passage runs something like: 'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order.'
The rhythmic anaphora of 'Dead' — repeated over and over — is both an incantation and an accusation.
He is pointing at every institution in Victorian England and saying: his blood is on your hands.
I find it almost unbearable to read. But I think that's exactly what Dickens intended.
I will not quarrel with the power of that passage — it is extraordinary.
But I want to place a gentle counter-pressure here.
The rhetorical brilliance of that apostrophe — 'Dead, your Majesty, Dead, my lords' — it is magnificent oratory.
But it is also, one must admit, somewhat self-congratulatory.
Dickens indicts the institutions — but Dickens is also performing his own virtue before an audience that largely agreed with him.
The real moral weight of the novel, to my mind, lies not in the apostrophe but in the smaller, quieter moments — Esther nursing Jo, Jarndyce's silent generosities.
Those are the places where Dickens trusts character more than rhetoric — and it is there that the novel transcends its polemical occasion.
I take Edmund's point — and I'll raise him Tom-all-Alone's itself.
Because the slum is where Dickens does something far more unsettling than apostrophe.
He makes the contagion literal. Smallpox spreads from Tom-all-Alone's through Esther — the disease crosses class lines.
Dickens understood something that the sanitary reformers were only beginning to grasp: that poverty is not quarantinable.
There's a passage about Tom-all-Alone's where Dickens writes of its 'pestiferous and obscene' condition — and how it will yet have its revenge on the fashionable world.
'Tom has his revenge. Even the winds are his messengers, and they serve him in these hours of darkness.'
That is not rhetoric. That is prophecy — and it carries a chill that the apostrophe, for all its brilliance, cannot quite match.
Oliver's reading of the contagion is absolutely right — and it connects to something I always notice on re-reading.
Dickens refuses to let the comfortable reader stay comfortable.
The novel's very structure mirrors its argument: Chancery infects everything, Tom-all-Alone's infects everything.
And the character who most embodies that refusal of comfort — for me — is not Jo but the brickmaker's wife, Jenny.
She has a dead baby on her lap when Esther and Ada visit, and she turns away Esther's well-meaning sympathy with absolute ferocity.
That refusal — that the poor are not obliged to be grateful, not obliged to be soft for our benefit — that is Dickens at his most honest.
The question of what we owe the poor — and what they owe us — sits at the centre of this novel in a way that still feels urgent.
Edmund, Caroline, Oliver — you've given us the social conscience of Bleak House in all its complexity: the rhetoric, the contagion, the dignity, the anger.
And what strikes me is that Dickens earns the anger precisely because he's also given us Jo alive — not just Jo dead and lamented.
In our next segment, we'll look at the novel's two narrators — Esther and the anonymous third-person voice — and ask what that formal choice means for how we experience all of this.

segments.title: Bleak House's Wit: Comedy in the Chaos

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' vast, magnificent, occasionally maddening novel and tries to understand why it still matters — and why it's still such extraordinary fun to read.
I'm joined today by three guests who know this book intimately, each from a rather different angle.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens scholars of his generation — a man who believes the novel's moral imagination is its greatest gift, and who reads it with the patience it deserves.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than any living performer, and brings to this conversation the irreplaceable gift of someone who has read every word aloud — who has felt the comic timing in the bones of the prose.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — someone whose relationship with this novel is frankly personal.
Today's subject is one that sometimes surprises people: Bleak House is genuinely, brilliantly funny.
How does Dickens sustain comic genius inside a novel of such darkness — and why does the comedy matter so much?

The thing people forget is that Bleak House was published in monthly parts — Dickens was essentially writing a television serial, and he knew his audience needed something to laugh at or they'd cancel their subscription.
But here's the thing — the comedy in this novel isn't relief from the darkness.
The comedy IS the darkness, wearing a different hat.
Take Grandfather Smallweed — that extraordinary, horrible, hilarious old man who is essentially a money-lending spider in human form.
Every scene he's in, he's being shaken and pummelled back into shape by his granddaughter — he keeps collapsing sideways in his chair.
It's physically absurd, it's genuinely funny — and it's also a portrait of pure, congealed, inhuman avarice.
He shouts — and Dickens gives him this magnificent line — he shouts at his wife: 'Shake me up, you brimstone chatterer!'
'Shake me up, you brimstone chatterer!'
Three words and you know exactly who this man is — and exactly what Dickens thinks of him.
What Oliver's describing is something I've thought about a great deal — Dickens uses the grotesque as a kind of moral shorthand.
The moment a character becomes physically absurd — starts collapsing, or talking in circles, or repeating themselves like a broken clockwork — you know their soul is in trouble.
But there's a separate current of comedy in this novel that I find almost more affecting — the comedy of Esther's narration.
Esther never thinks she's being funny — and that's precisely what makes her funny.

When she describes the Jellybys' household — the chaos, the children tumbling downstairs, Mrs Jellyby dictating letters about the people of Borrioboola-Gha with perfect serenity while everything burns around her —
Esther simply records it all with mild, baffled courtesy.
She is the straight-woman to half the cast, and she doesn't even know it.

Dickens gives her a line that I've underlined in every copy I own — she says of Mrs Jellyby: 'I was feeling so fresh and pleasant after the journey that I was rather disappointed in her personal appearance.'
'I was feeling so fresh and pleasant after the journey that I was rather disappointed in her personal appearance.'
'Rather disappointed.' That devastating understatement is pure Esther — and pure Dickens.
I think both my colleagues are right, though I might frame it rather differently.
The comic figures in Bleak House are not merely funny — they are, in the deepest sense, cautionary.
Consider the Reverend Chadband — that magnificent, oleaginous fraud who speaks entirely in self-important biblical cadences that mean precisely nothing.
Dickens was, I think, profoundly suspicious of eloquence detached from genuine feeling — and Chadband is the apotheosis of that suspicion.
He has that famous passage where Chadband holds forth on Jo the crossing-sweeper — and it is one of the most withering things in the novel.
'My young friend,' says Chadband, 'you are to us a pearl, you are to us a diamond, you are to us a gem, you are to us a jewel.'
And of course Jo has no idea what any of this means — he is hungry and cold and thoroughly bewildered.
The comedy and the cruelty arrive in the same sentence.
That is not, I think, an accident — it is a deliberate artistic strategy of the highest order.
Edmund's put his finger on something absolutely central — the comedy in this novel is never innocent.
And as a performer, I can tell you: Chadband is the most treacherous character to read aloud in all of Dickens.
Because if you play him too broad — too obviously ridiculous — you lose the menace.
And if you play him too straight, the audience doesn't realise they're allowed to laugh.
There's a tonal needle Dickens threads constantly in this novel — and it's extraordinarily difficult to sustain.
But then you get a character like Mr Turveydrop — that magnificent, preposterous monument to Deportment — and the comedy is purer, lighter.
Dickens describes him as a model of Deportment — capital D — and everything about him is described in terms of his magnificent, useless self-presentation.
He is one of Dickens' great comic vanities — utterly hollow, utterly confident, utterly absurd.
Turveydrop is one of my great loves in this novel — because Dickens is so precise about which kind of funny he is.
He's not cruel, like Smallweed.
He's not dangerous, like Chadband.
He's simply a man who has made himself into a work of decorative art — and requires everyone around him to maintain the exhibit.
Dickens describes him as having a 'coat, hat, gloves, and cravat — all of the very newest and most beautiful fashion.'
'He was not young, and his figure was not good, but he was got up with such consummate art that it looked uncommonly well.'
'Got up with consummate art.' There is so much in that phrase — the effort, the vanity, the performance of a self that isn't really there.
And then his long-suffering son Prince dances himself into exhaustion to support this magnificent fraud of a father.
It's funny and it's sad — and Dickens doesn't force you to choose which.
That simultaneous comedy and pathos is, I would argue, the central achievement of the novel's comic register.
One thinks of Johnson's remark that the only end of writing is to enable the reader better to enjoy life, or better to endure it.
Dickens' comedy does both — sometimes in the same sentence.
What I think is often underestimated is the comic precision of the third-person narrator — who is quite a different voice from Esther's.
The third-person narrator is capable of a kind of dry, almost glacial irony that Esther, in her goodness, could never manage.
Think of the opening of the novel — that extraordinary set piece about Chancery — where Dickens writes of the Lord Chancellor: 'The Lord Chancellor is, somewhat difficultly, looking at a Fog.'
'On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be sitting here — as here he is — with a foggy glory round his head.'
'Foggy glory.' Two words, and the entire institution of Chancery is mocked — not with rage, but with something colder and more deadly: wit.
'Foggy glory' — I think that might be the two most devastating words in a novel full of devastating words.
What strikes me listening to all three of you is that the comedy in Bleak House isn't decoration — it's load-bearing.
Take it away and the novel collapses — or becomes unbearable.
In our next section we'll turn to the novel's darkness — the suffering that the comedy holds at bay — and ask whether Dickens earns his own bleakness.

segments.title: The System's Victims and the Reader's Complicity

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent some time with the fog, the Court of Chancery, and Dickens' extraordinary opening.
Now I want to turn to something that sits at the very heart of the novel — the question of who suffers, and what our role as readers might be in that suffering.
Bleak House is full of victims — Jo the crossing-sweeper, Miss Flite, Richard Carstone, even Lady Dedlock — but Dickens does something remarkable with them.
He makes us complicit — not just observers, but participants in the indifference he's indicting.
Edmund, Oliver, Caroline — I think this is where the novel's moral charge really lives.
You raise precisely the right question, and it is one that has occupied serious readers of the novel for a very long time.
Dickens understood — with a novelist's instinct that no social pamphleteer could match — that indignation without implication is merely noise.
Consider Jo — perhaps the most devastating figure in all of Victorian fiction.
He is a crossing-sweeper — a child who knows nothing, owns nothing, and is wanted by nobody.
And yet Dickens gives him this repeated, heartbreaking refrain — the authorities are always moving him on.
"Move on, Jo, move on. There's nothing here for you."
Every institution in the novel says exactly the same thing to Jo — the law, the church, the charitable societies.
And the reader, sitting comfortably with the novel in hand, is being asked: are you not doing precisely the same?
Edmund has gone straight to the right place, and I'm glad he did.
What strikes me every time I re-read the Jo chapters is how deliberately Dickens refuses to let us stay comfortable.
He addresses the reader directly — breaks the fourth wall, we might say — when Jo is dying.
He writes — and this passage never fails to stop me entirely —
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order."
"Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That catalogue — Your Majesty, lords, reverends, men and women — it's everyone.
You cannot find a gap in that list to slip through as an innocent bystander.
Dickens has stitched you into the indictment.
Having read that passage — oh, I should say performed it — perhaps four hundred times, it still lands like a blow.
Every single time.
What Dickens has done technically there is extraordinary — that anaphora, that drumbeat of "Dead" — it's a funeral toll built out of pure syntax.
As a performer, you discover very quickly that you cannot hurry it.
Each "Dead" must land, must breathe, must cost something before you move to the next.
But I want to say something about complicity that goes a little beyond Jo, if I may.
There's a subtler trap Dickens sets — and it involves Mrs. Jellyby.
We laugh at her — we're meant to laugh at her — this woman of perpetual correspondence who cannot see the children falling down the stairs.
But the laugh is the trap.
Because the reader who chuckles at Mrs. Jellyby's distant philanthropy has just demonstrated exactly the comfortable distance that Dickens is indicting throughout the whole novel.
Oliver, that is — and I use this word carefully — a genuinely penetrating observation.
Dickens is far too great a novelist to offer us a simple villain and a simple escape.
Mrs. Jellyby is, in one sense, a caricature — that fixed gaze at something far away, never quite resolving into the present.
Dickens describes her eyes as having "a curious habit of seeming to look a long way off, as if they could see nothing nearer than Africa."
Quite marvellous.
But I would add — and here is where I part company slightly from purely political readings — that Richard Carstone is perhaps the more searching indictment.
Because Richard is destroyed not by poverty, not by indifference, but by his own surrender to hope — to the Chancery suit as a kind of opium.
The system does not merely grind the poor under its wheels — it seduces the comfortable into ruin as well.
Richard haunts me every time.
He comes in full of energy and charm — the kind of young man you'd want at a dinner table — and the novel slowly turns him to ash.
Jarndyce warns him — again and again — with extraordinary patience.
There's that line Jarndyce speaks — it's almost unbearable in its gentleness —
"Suffer no fancy to mislead you. It is a place of ruin. There is ruin in it for every soul that touches it."
And Richard nods, and smiles, and is certain he will be the exception.
The reader aches, because we've seen this before — in life, in other novels.
We know exactly where this road goes.
And our helplessness to stop him — that is the reader's complicity made utterly, painfully private.
There's a moment in the later chapters where Richard looks at Jarndyce — his guardian, his benefactor, the best man he knows — and is convinced Jarndyce is working against him.
The suit has metastasized into his thinking so completely that generosity itself looks like treachery.
Now, when you perform that section, the temptation is to play Richard as simply foolish.
But Dickens won't let you do that — he keeps giving Richard these flashes of genuine self-awareness.
He writes of Richard looking pale and worn, knowing something is wrong, but utterly unable to stop.
That is the particular cruelty — the system doesn't just consume you; it leaves you watching yourself be consumed.
And then there is Miss Flite — who got there before Richard, who has been watching herself be consumed for decades.
She keeps her birds in cages — Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness.
She means to release them when the suit is decided.
It's one of the most beautiful and terrible images in all of Dickens — all of that lost life, caged and catalogued and waiting.
Miss Flite is a figure I confess I once slightly undervalued — dismissed, perhaps, as merely one grotesque among many.
I was wrong.
She is a prospective mirror — Richard and Ada see in her what the court will make of them, if they let it.
And she is perfectly aware of this function — she tells them so, in her oblique, damaged way.
She says something to the effect that she was a ward in Jarndyce for many years, that she has been expecting judgement every day, and that she was a little mad when she first came.
"Only a little then," she says — and the comedy and the tragedy are entirely inseparable.
The reader laughs — and then realises they are laughing at the ruins of a life, and the laugh curdles.
That curdling — that's exactly the experience Dickens engineers.
He gives you the pleasure of comedy, and then turns it in your hands so it cuts.
Lady Dedlock works differently — she's a victim of a much older, more aristocratic machinery.
But there's a moment — when she flees Chesney Wold, when she's found dead at the gate of the burial ground in Nemo's parish — that the novel collapses all distance.
Dickens describes Esther finding her there, dressed in the clothes of a brickmaker's wife.
The great lady of Chesney Wold, dead in rags, at the gate of the graveyard where her secret is buried.
The novel offers no comfort there — no redemptive arc, no mercy from the system she'd served and been served by.
And we, the readers, knew it was coming, because the fog told us at the very beginning.
That is such a powerful set of observations — the fog as prologue to all of this catastrophe.

What I'm hearing is that the reader's complicity operates on several levels at once — the laughter we give Dickens, the comfort we take in Esther's goodness, even the suspense we enjoy as the plot unfolds.
All of it implicates us in a world that is producing Jo, producing Miss Flite, producing Lady Dedlock's end.
Coming up, we'll turn to Esther herself — the one character through whose eyes we see much of this suffering — and ask what it means to narrate goodness in the middle of so much ruin.

segments.title: Threads Converge: Narrative Mastery and Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: We've spent this episode pulling at the threads of Bleak House — the fog, the Court, the characters caught in its machinery.
Now, in this final segment, I want to ask each of you: how does Dickens pull those threads together?
And what kind of moral reckoning does this novel finally demand of us?
What strikes me, looking at the whole architecture of this novel, is how ruthlessly Dickens engineers his convergences.
Richard Carstone's destruction, for instance, does not arrive as a sudden catastrophe — it is the slow, terrible flowering of a flaw we have watched from the very beginning.
Dickens is almost Aristotelian in his sense that character is fate.
Richard does not simply fall victim to Chancery — he surrenders to it, which is an altogether more damning verdict.

When we reach that final scene in court, and Jarndyce and Jarndyce is declared concluded because the entire estate has been consumed in costs, Dickens gives us his great punch line delivered absolutely straight.
"The costs have swallowed up the whole."
Four words of summary for decades of human wreckage.
That is the novel's moral geometry laid absolutely bare.
Edmund, I think you've put your finger on something that gets overlooked in all the grand thematic readings — the sheer comic perfection of that moment.
Because it is funny, in the blackest possible way.
The whole edifice of legal ceremony, the wigs, the Latin, the centuries of solemnity — and the punchline is that there's nothing left.
Dickens had been building toward that joke since page one, and he lands it with absolute deadpan authority.
But I want to also speak for the other convergence — the one that breaks your heart rather than makes you laugh.
Richard and Ada. Those two poor beautiful young people who began the novel with everything before them.
And Dickens writes Richard's death with a restraint that is almost unbearable — he simply has him say that the cause is won at last, meaning the lawsuit, in his last delirium.
"The clouds have cleared away, and it is bright now."
He thinks he's won. He dies thinking he's won.
It is one of the cruellest things Dickens ever wrote, and also one of the most merciful.
Oliver, that parallel haunts me — the two convergences, the comic and the tragic, running side by side to the final pages.
But for me the moral reckoning of this novel lives most completely in Esther's voice, in what she chooses not to say.
She is the most scrupulous narrator Dickens ever created — endlessly qualifying, endlessly deferring, endlessly doubting her own perceptions.
And yet the novel's moral weight accumulates precisely through her goodness — a goodness that is never sentimentalised because she never claims it herself.
There's a moment near the end where she describes herself after the illness has marked her face, and she looks in a mirror and writes something that has stayed with me across every re-reading.
"I was very well pleased to think that I was so much better."
That's it. That's her entire response to having her face changed forever.
The restraint is staggering. And because Dickens has earned our trust in Esther's voice over eight hundred pages, that line does more work than a paragraph of lamentation ever could.
Caroline touches on something that I think separates Bleak House from Dickens' other great novels — the question of what heroism looks like in a world so thoroughly corrupted.
The Court cannot be reformed within the timeframe of the novel — Dickens offers us no Oliver Twist rescue, no Nicholas Nickleby triumph.
What he offers instead is Jarndyce's extraordinary act of renunciation — standing aside for Woodcourt, giving up Esther because her happiness demands it.
Burke would have recognised it. It is not heroism as conquest but heroism as the quiet mastery of one's own desires.
And Dickens frames it beautifully — Jarndyce has renovated a cottage for them, named it Bleak House, and when he brings Esther to it, he tells her it was always meant to be hers.
"This is your home, my dear — earned by years of goodness."
The Court takes everything and gives nothing back — but Jarndyce gives everything and takes nothing.
That is Dickens' moral architecture: held together not by systems but by persons.
And yet Edmund — and I say this with great admiration — I wonder if the novel itself is slightly uneasy about that resolution.
Because Dickens returns to the third-person narrator for the very last word — Esther doesn't close the novel alone.
The impersonal voice steps back in to tell us about the world beyond Esther's cottage, about Tom-all-Alone's still standing, about Jo's kind still dying in the streets.
And that's Dickens refusing to let the personal redemption close out the social indictment.
The passage about Jo — earlier in the novel, before his death — is the one I find I have to stop reading aloud because my voice goes.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
That passage doesn't ask for sympathy — it demands an accounting.
It is the most furious thing Dickens ever wrote, in the calmest possible voice.
Oliver has it exactly right, and I think it's why the novel can't be resolved into a single verdict.
Bleak House holds its contradictions deliberately — the private happiness and the public outrage live together, unreconciled, by design.
And what I love most, on a purely craft level, is how Dickens ties the two narrative strands together not through plot mechanics but through image.
The fog of the opening chapter never quite lifts — it reappears throughout, thinner perhaps, never gone.
But the last image Dickens grants Esther is light — the new Bleak House in sunshine, the children running, her husband looking at her with the same love he showed when she was changed.
And Esther, characteristically, questions even that happiness — she breaks off and says she can hardly believe she could be lovelier than before.
"But I know that my dearest little pets are very pretty, and that my darling is very beautiful, and that my husband is very handsome."
She deflects the question onto everyone around her. She still won't claim anything for herself.
Even at the very end of the novel, Esther Summerson is the same person she was at the beginning — and that consistency, that moral constancy, is Dickens' truest answer to Chancery.
Edmund, a final thought — you've argued throughout that the novel is ultimately about individual character.
Does Bleak House end by vindicating that reading, or does it — as Oliver suggests — leave the question dangerously open?
I think it does both, and I mean that as the highest possible compliment to Dickens' intelligence.
He was not a systematic thinker — he was something far more valuable: a supreme moral observer.
The novel ends in that magnificent double exposure: the fog still present in the world, and Esther's small light burning against it.
That is not a contradiction — that is the truth of how we actually live.
Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, Caroline Woodcourt — what an extraordinary conversation this has been.
We set out to unpack a novel that spans a thousand pages, two narrators, and more characters than some novelists manage in a lifetime.
What we've found, I think, is that Bleak House earns its reputation not despite its complexity but because of it.
The fog never entirely clears. The Court grinds on. But Esther keeps her accounts, and that — Dickens insists — is not nothing.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked. We hope the fog has lifted, at least a little.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and

down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.

I felt this to be true; though if I may venture to mention what I
thought besides, I thought it much to be regretted that Richard’s
education had not counteracted those influences or directed his
character. He had been eight years at a public school and had learnt,
I understood, to make Latin verses of several sorts in the most
admirable manner. But I never heard that it had been anybody’s
business to find out what his natural bent was, or where his failings
lay, or to adapt any kind of knowledge to HIM. HE had been adapted to
the verses and had learnt the art of making them to such perfection
that if he had remained at school until he was of age, I suppose he
could only have gone on making them over and over again unless he had
enlarged his education by forgetting how to do it. Still, although I
had no doubt that they were very beautiful, and very improving, and
very sufficient for a great many purposes of life, and always
remembered all through life, I did doubt whether Richard would not
have profited by some one studying him a little, instead of his
studying them quite so much.

c36:p11.text:
Wishing to be fully re-established in my strength and my good spirits
before Ada came, I now laid down a little series of plans with
Charley for being in the fresh air all day long. We were to be out
before breakfast, and were to dine early, and were to be out again
before and after dinner, and were to talk in the garden after tea,
and were to go to rest betimes, and were to climb every hill and
explore every road, lane, and field in the neighbourhood. As to
restoratives and strengthening delicacies, Mr. Boythorn’s good
housekeeper was for ever trotting about with something to eat or
drink in her hand; I could not even be heard of as resting in the
park but she would come trotting after me with a basket, her cheerful
face shining with a lecture on the importance of frequent
nourishment. Then there was a pony expressly for my riding, a chubby
pony with a short neck and a mane all over his eyes who could
canter—when he would—so easily and quietly that he was a treasure.
In a very few days he would come to me in the paddock when I called
him, and eat out of my hand, and follow me about. We arrived at such
a capital understanding that when he was jogging with me lazily, and
rather obstinately, down some shady lane, if I patted his neck and
said, “Stubbs, I am surprised you don’t canter when you know how much
I like it; and I think you might oblige me, for you are only getting
stupid and going to sleep,” he would give his head a comical shake or
two and set off directly, while Charley would stand still and laugh
with such enjoyment that her laughter was like music. I don’t know
who had given Stubbs his name, but it seemed to belong to him as
naturally as his rough coat. Once we put him in a little chaise and
drove him triumphantly through the green lanes for five miles; but
all at once, as we were extolling him to the skies, he seemed to take
it ill that he should have been accompanied so far by the circle of
tantalizing little gnats that had been hovering round and round his
ears the whole way without appearing to advance an inch, and stopped
to think about it. I suppose he came to the decision that it was not
to be borne, for he steadily refused to move until I gave the reins
to Charley and got out and walked, when he followed me with a sturdy
sort of good humour, putting his head under my arm and rubbing his
ear against my sleeve. It was in vain for me to say, “Now, Stubbs, I
feel quite sure from what I know of you that you will go on if I ride
a little while,” for the moment I left him, he stood stock still
again. Consequently I was obliged to lead the way, as before; and in
this order we returned home, to the great delight of the village.
c36:p11.summary: Esther establishes a recovery routine with Charley, exploring the countryside and developing a whimsical friendship with a stubbornly independent pony named Stubbs.

Caddy was not at all deficient in natural affection for her mother,
but mentioned this with tears as an undeniable fact, which I am
afraid it was. We were sorry for the poor dear girl and found so much
to admire in the good disposition which had survived under such
discouragement that we both at once (I mean Ada and I) proposed a
little scheme that made her perfectly joyful. This was her staying
with us for three weeks, my staying with her for one, and our all
three contriving and cutting out, and repairing, and sewing, and
saving, and doing the very best we could think of to make the most of

we took her home next day to arrange the matter and brought her out
again in triumph with her boxes and all the purchases that could be
squeezed out of a ten-pound note, which Mr. Jellyby had found in the
docks I suppose, but which he at all events gave her. What my
guardian would not have given her if we had encouraged him, it would
be difficult to say, but we thought it right to compound for no more
than her wedding-dress and bonnet. He agreed to this compromise, and
if Caddy had ever been happy in her life, she was happy when we sat

“At a rough kind of fellow—a sort of human hedgehog rolled up,” said
Mr. Skimpole, “who is a baker in this neighbourhood and from whom we
borrowed a couple of arm-chairs. We wanted a couple of arm-chairs,
and we hadn’t got them, and therefore of course we looked to a man
who HAD got them, to lend them. Well! This morose person lent them,
and we wore them out. When they were worn out, he wanted them back.
He had them back. He was contented, you will say. Not at all. He
objected to their being worn. I reasoned with him, and pointed out
his mistake. I said, ‘Can you, at your time of life, be so
headstrong, my friend, as to persist that an arm-chair is a thing to
put upon a shelf and look at? That it is an object to contemplate, to
survey from a distance, to consider from a point of sight? Don’t you
KNOW that these arm-chairs were borrowed to be sat upon?’ He was
unreasonable and unpersuadable and used intemperate language. Being
as patient as I am at this minute, I addressed another appeal to him.
I said, ‘Now, my good man, however our business capacities may vary,
we are all children of one great mother, Nature. On this blooming
summer morning here you see me’ (I was on the sofa) ‘with flowers
before me, fruit upon the table, the cloudless sky above me, the air
full of fragrance, contemplating Nature. I entreat you, by our common
brotherhood, not to interpose between me and a subject so sublime,
the absurd figure of an angry baker!’ But he did,” said Mr. Skimpole,
raising his laughing eyes in playful astonishment; “he did interpose
that ridiculous figure, and he does, and he will again. And therefore
I am very glad to get out of his way and to go home with my friend
Jarndyce.”

c48:p128.text:
A very quiet night. When the moon shines very brilliantly, a solitude
and stillness seem to proceed from her that influence even crowded
places full of life. Not only is it a still night on dusty high roads
and on hill-summits, whence a wide expanse of country may be seen in
repose, quieter and quieter as it spreads away into a fringe of trees
against the sky with the grey ghost of a bloom upon them; not only is
it a still night in gardens and in woods, and on the river where the
water-meadows are fresh and green, and the stream sparkles on among
pleasant islands, murmuring weirs, and whispering rushes; not only
does the stillness attend it as it flows where houses cluster thick,
where many bridges are reflected in it, where wharves and shipping
make it black and awful, where it winds from these disfigurements
through marshes whose grim beacons stand like skeletons washed
ashore, where it expands through the bolder region of rising grounds,
rich in cornfield wind-mill and steeple, and where it mingles with
the ever-heaving sea; not only is it a still night on the deep, and
on the shore where the watcher stands to see the ship with her spread
wings cross the path of light that appears to be presented to only
him; but even on this stranger’s wilderness of London there is some
rest. Its steeples and towers and its one great dome grow more
ethereal; its smoky house-tops lose their grossness in the pale
effulgence; the noises that arise from the streets are fewer and are
softened, and the footsteps on the pavements pass more tranquilly
away. In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn’s inhabiting, where the
shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their
sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them
exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a
distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.
c48:p128.summary: The narrator provides an extended, elaborate description of moonlit calm across the natural world, from countryside to ocean, ending with Chancery metaphors for Tulkinghorn's world.
c48:p128.best_quote: In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”
c51:p27.summary: Richard confesses to Woodcourt that he has accomplished nothing, lacks purpose, and feels trapped by fate and the Chancery suit, yet demands acceptance without judgment.
c51:p27.best_quote: I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not.

c15:p44.text:
He looked at Ada, and at Mr. Jarndyce, and at Mr. Skimpole, fixing
the same angry stare on each in succession as they passed and
followed me. Mr. Jarndyce gave him good day. “Good day!” he said
abruptly and fiercely. He was a tall, sallow man with a careworn head
on which but little hair remained, a deeply lined face, and prominent
eyes. He had a combative look and a chafing, irritable manner which,
associated with his figure—still large and powerful, though
evidently in its decline—rather alarmed me. He had a pen in his
hand, and in the glimpse I caught of his room in passing, I saw that
it was covered with a litter of papers.
c15:p44.summary: Esther observes Gridley's physical appearance—tall, sallow, careworn, deeply lined, with prominent eyes and a combative manner—and notes his room is covered with papers.
c15:p44.best_quote: He had a combative look and a chafing, irritable manner which, associated with his figure—still large and powerful, though evidently in its decline—rather alarmed me.

c44:p33.text:
It was not a love letter, though it expressed so much love, but was
written just as he would at any time have spoken to me. I saw his
face, and heard his voice, and felt the influence of his kind
protecting manner in every line. It addressed me as if our places
were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the
feelings they had awakened his. It dwelt on my being young, and he
past the prime of life; on his having attained a ripe age, while I
was a child; on his writing to me with a silvered head, and knowing
all this so well as to set it in full before me for mature
deliberation. It told me that I would gain nothing by such a marriage
and lose nothing by rejecting it, for no new relation could enhance
the tenderness in which he held me, and whatever my decision was, he
was certain it would be right. But he had considered this step anew
since our late confidence and had decided on taking it, if it only
served to show me through one poor instance that the whole world
would readily unite to falsify the stern prediction of my childhood.
I was the last to know what happiness I could bestow upon him, but of
that he said no more, for I was always to remember that I owed him
nothing and that he was my debtor, and for very much. He had often
thought of our future, and foreseeing that the time must come, and
fearing that it might come soon, when Ada (now very nearly of age)
would leave us, and when our present mode of life must be broken up,
had become accustomed to reflect on this proposal. Thus he made it.
If I felt that I could ever give him the best right he could have to
be my protector, and if I felt that I could happily and justly become
the dear companion of his remaining life, superior to all lighter
chances and changes than death, even then he could not have me bind
myself irrevocably while this letter was yet so new to me, but even
then I must have ample time for reconsideration. In that case, or in
the opposite case, let him be unchanged in his old relation, in his
old manner, in the old name by which I called him. And as to his
bright Dame Durden and little housekeeper, she would ever be the
same, he knew.
c44:p33.summary: Esther recounts the substance of Jarndyce's letter: it is written with selfless love and deference; he emphasizes her youth versus his age, her disfigurement versus his devotion, that she owes him nothing, and that if she accepts, he asks only that she reconsider with time and remain as she is.
c44:p33.best_quote: It addressed me as if our places were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the feelings they had awakened his.

c44:p57.text:
I put my two arms round his neck and kissed him, and he said was this
the mistress of Bleak House, and I said yes; and it made no
difference presently, and we all went out together, and I said
nothing to my precious pet about it.
c44:p57.summary: Esther embraces Jarndyce and accepts his proposal by kissing him; he confirms she is to be mistress of Bleak House, and the three depart together, with Esther keeping the engagement from Ada.
c44:p57.best_quote: I put my two arms round his neck and kissed him, and he said was this the mistress of Bleak House, and I said yes

c40:p94.text:
“The lady was wealthy and beautiful, and had a liking for the girl,
and treated her with great kindness, and kept her always near her.
Now this lady preserved a secret under all her greatness, which she
had preserved for many years. In fact, she had in early life been
engaged to marry a young rake—he was a captain in the army—nothing
connected with whom came to any good. She never did marry him, but
she gave birth to a child of which he was the father.”
c40:p94.summary: The lady preserved a secret: she had an illegitimate child with an army officer in her youth, which she never married.
c40:p94.best_quote: she had in early life been engaged to marry a young rake—he was a captain in the army—nothing connected with whom came to any good. She never did marry him, but she gave birth to a child of which he was the father

c40:p96.text:
“The captain in the army being dead, she believed herself safe; but a
train of circumstances with which I need not trouble you led to
discovery. As I received the story, they began in an imprudence on
her own part one day when she was taken by surprise, which shows how
difficult it is for the firmest of us (she was very firm) to be
always guarded. There was great domestic trouble and amazement, you
may suppose; I leave you to imagine, Sir Leicester, the husband’s
grief. But that is not the present point. When Mr. Rouncewell’s
townsman heard of the disclosure, he no more allowed the girl to be
patronized and honoured than he would have suffered her to be trodden
underfoot before his eyes. Such was his pride, that he indignantly
took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of
the honour done him and his daughter by the lady’s condescension; not
the least. He resented the girl’s position, as if the lady had been
the commonest of commoners. That is the story. I hope Lady Dedlock
will excuse its painful nature.”
c40:p96.summary: The captain being dead, the secret was exposed through the lady's imprudence. The working-class man learned of his daughter's patronage and angrily withdrew her, refusing aristocratic condescension.
c40:p96.best_quote: Such was his pride, that he indignantly took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of the honour done him and his daughter by the lady's condescension; not the least. He resented the girl's position, as if the lady had been the commonest of commoners.

c10:p66.text:
For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and
trousers, with bare feet. He has a yellow look in the spectral
darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of
its wick (still burning) has doubled over and left a tower of
winding-sheet above it. His hair is ragged, mingling with his
whiskers and his beard—the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the
scum and mist around him, in neglect. Foul and filthy as the room is,
foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes
those are which most oppress the senses in it; but through the
general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco,
there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.

I applied the key on hearing this and opened the door. In a poor room
with a sloping ceiling and containing very little furniture was a
mite of a boy, some five or six years old, nursing and hushing a
heavy child of eighteen months. There was no fire, though the weather
was cold; both children were wrapped in some poor shawls and tippets

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

c15:p107.text:
“Mr. Jarndyce,” said Gridley with a rough sort of salutation, “you
bear your wrongs more quietly than I can bear mine. More than that, I
tell you—and I tell this gentleman, and these young ladies, if they
are friends of yours—that if I took my wrongs in any other way, I
should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging
them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get,
that I am able to keep my wits together. It is only that!” he said,
speaking in a homely, rustic way and with great vehemence. “You may
tell me that I over-excite myself. I answer that it’s in my nature to
do it, under wrong, and I must do it. There’s nothing between doing
it, and sinking into the smiling state of the poor little mad woman
that haunts the court. If I was once to sit down under it, I should
become imbecile.”
c15:p107.summary: Gridley explains that his rage is essential to his sanity; without the outlet of resenting and avenging his wrongs in thought, he would become imbecile like 'the poor little mad woman that haunts the court.'
c15:p107.best_quote: if I took my wrongs in any other way, I should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get, that I am able to keep my wits together.

c5:p56.text:
“Aye!” said the old man, coming slowly out of his abstraction. “Yes!
Tom Jarndyce—you’ll excuse me, being related; but he was never known
about court by any other name, and was as well known there as—she is
now,” nodding slightly at his lodger. “Tom Jarndyce was often in
here. He got into a restless habit of strolling about when the cause
was on, or expected, talking to the little shopkeepers and telling
’em to keep out of Chancery, whatever they did. ‘For,’ says he, ‘it’s
being ground to bits in a slow mill; it’s being roasted at a slow
fire; it’s being stung to death by single bees; it’s being drowned by
drops; it’s going mad by grains.’ He was as near making away with
himself, just where the young lady stands, as near could be.”
c5:p56.summary: Krook relates the tragic story of Tom Jarndyce, the original plaintiff in the suit, who repeatedly warned others to avoid Chancery's destruction. Tom became suicidal and eventually shot himself at a tavern near Chancery Lane.
c5:p56.best_quote: For, says he, it's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains.

c5:p58.text:
“He come in at the door,” said the old man, slowly pointing an
imaginary track along the shop, “on the day he did it—the whole
neighbourhood had said for months before that he would do it, of a
certainty sooner or later—he come in at the door that day, and
walked along there, and sat himself on a bench that stood there, and
asked me (you’ll judge I was a mortal sight younger then) to fetch
him a pint of wine. ‘For,’ says he, ‘Krook, I am much depressed; my
cause is on again, and I think I’m nearer judgment than I ever was.’
I hadn’t a mind to leave him alone; and I persuaded him to go to the
tavern over the way there, t’other side my lane (I mean Chancery
Lane); and I followed and looked in at the window, and saw him,
comfortable as I thought, in the arm-chair by the fire, and company
with him. I hadn’t hardly got back here when I heard a shot go
echoing and rattling right away into the inn. I ran out—neighbours
ran out—twenty of us cried at once, ‘Tom Jarndyce!’”
c5:p58.summary: Krook describes in vivid detail Tom Jarndyce's final day: how he came into the shop depressed, asked for wine, was persuaded to go to a tavern, and then shot himself. The neighbourhood had long predicted this tragedy.
c5:p58.best_quote: For, says he, Krook, I am much depressed; my cause is on again, and I think I'm nearer judgment than I ever was.
